evidence: Caes. B.C. 3.13: jūrat sē eum nōn dēsertūrum (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Off. 3.108: falsum jūrāre, to swear falsely (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: What one swears follows in the accusative and infinitive. Jūrātus, having sworn, is “on oath”; injūrātus, “unsworn” (Plaut. Am. 281).

evidence: Cic. Off. 3.104: est enim jūs jūrandum affirmātiō religiōsa (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Also written as one word. Jūs jūrandum dare, to give one’s oath; jūs jūrandum adigere aliquem (Caes. B.C. 1.76) and jūre jūrandō adigere (Liv. 21.1.4), to make someone swear; jūs jūrandum cōnservāre, to keep it (Cic. Off. 3.100).

terms.gloss: swear solemnly, swear by the gods
terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; later Gell.
evidence: Plaut. Cas. 3.5.37: per omnēs deōs et deās dējerāvit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Morgan–Owens, after Vives, gives it for swearing in the sense of bad language; classically it is only taking an oath (Lewis & Short). For swearing at someone, see abuse.

phrases.latin: altāribus admōtum tāctīs sacrīs jūre jūrandō adāctum sē cum prīmum posset hostem fore populō Rōmānō
phrases.english: brought to the altar, his hand on the offerings, he was made to swear that as soon as he could he would be an enemy of Rome
